A gentle joyousness—a mighty mildness of repose in swiftness, invested the gliding whale. Not the white bull Jupiter swimming away with ravished Europa clinging to his graceful horns; his lovely, leering eyes sideways intent upon the maid; with smooth bewitching fleetness, rippling straight for the nuptial bower in Crete; not Jove, not that great majesty Supreme! did surpass the glorified White Whale as he so divinely swam.

On each soft side—coincident with the parted swell, that but once leaving him, then flowed so wide away—on each bright side, the whale shed off enticings. No wonder there had been some among the hunters who namelessly transported and allured by all this serenity, had ventured to assail it; but had fatally found that quietude but the vesture of tornadoes. And thus, through the serene tranquillities of the tropical sea, among waves whose hand-clappings were suspended by exceeding rapture, Moby Dick moved on, still withholding from sight the full terrors of his submerged trunk, entirely hiding the wrenched hideousness of his jaw. But soon the fore part of him slowly rose from the water; for an instant his whole marbleized body formed a high arch, like Virginia’s Natural Bridge, and warningly waving his bannered flukes in the air, the grand god revealed himself, sounded, and went out of sight. Hoveringly halting, and dipping on the wing, the white sea-fowls longingly lingered over the agitated pool that he left.
With oars apeak, and paddles down, the sheets of their sails adrift, the three boats now stilly floated, awaiting Moby Dick’s reappearance.

“An hour,” said Ahab, standing rooted in his boat’s stern; and he gazed beyond the whale’s place, towards the dim blue spaces and wide wooing vacancies to leeward. It was only an instant; for again his eyes seemed whirling round in his head as he swept the watery circle. The breeze now freshened; the sea began to swell.
“The birds!—the birds!” cried Tashtego.

In long Indian file, as when herons take wing, the white birds were now all flying towards Ahab’s boat; and when within a few yards began fluttering over the water there, wheeling round and round, with joyous, expectant cries. Their vision was keener than man’s; Ahab could discover no sign in the sea. But suddenly as he peered down and down into its depths, he profoundly saw a white living spot no bigger than a white weasel, with wonderful celerity uprising, and magnifying as it rose, till it turned, and then there were plainly revealed two long crooked rows of white, glistening teeth, floating up from the undiscoverable bottom. It was Moby Dick’s open mouth and scrolled jaw; his vast, shadowed bulk still half blending with the blue of the sea. The glittering mouth yawned beneath the boat like an open-doored marble tomb; and giving one sidelong sweep with his steering oar, Ahab whirled the craft aside from this tremendous apparition. Then, calling upon Fedallah to change places with him, went forward to the bows, and seizing Perth’s harpoon, commanded his crew to grasp their oars and stand by to stern.

Now, by reason of this timely spinning round the boat upon its axis, its bow, by anticipation, was made to face the whale’s head while yet under water. But as if perceiving this stratagem, Moby Dick, with that malicious intelligence ascribed to him, sidelingly transplanted himself, as it were, in an instant, shooting his pleated head lengthwise beneath the boat.

Through and through; through every plank and each rib, it thrilled for an instant, the whale obliquely lying on his back, in the manner of a biting shark, slowly and feelingly taking its bows full within his mouth, so that the long, narrow, scrolled lower jaw curled high up into the open air, and one of the teeth caught in a row-lock. The bluish pearl-white of the inside of the jaw was within six inches of Ahab’s head, and reached higher than that. In this attitude the White Whale now shook the slight cedar as a mildly cruel cat her mouse. With unastonished eyes Fedallah gazed, and crossed his arms; but the tiger-yellow crew were tumbling over each other’s heads to gain the uttermost stern.

And now, while both elastic gunwales were springing in and out, as the whale dallied with the doomed craft in this devilish way; and from his body being submerged beneath the boat, he could not be darted at from the bows, for the bows were almost inside of him, as it were; and while the other boats involuntarily paused, as before a quick crisis impossible to withstand, then it was that monomaniac Ahab, furious with this tantalizing vicinity of his foe, which placed him all alive and helpless in the very jaws he hated; frenzied with all this, he seized the long bone with his naked hands, and wildly strove to wrench it from its gripe. As now he thus vainly strove, the jaw slipped from him; the frail gunwales bent in, collapsed, and snapped, as both jaws, like an enormous shears, sliding further aft, bit the craft completely in twain, and locked themselves fast again in the sea, midway between the two floating wrecks. These floated aside, the broken ends drooping, the crew at the stern-wreck clinging to the gunwales, and striving to hold fast to the oars to lash them across.

At that preluding moment, ere the boat was yet snapped, Ahab, the first to perceive the whale’s intent, by the crafty upraising of his head, a movement that loosed his hold for the time; at that moment his hand had made one final effort to push the boat out of the bite. But only slipping further into the whale’s mouth, and tilting over sideways as it slipped, the boat had shaken off his hold on the jaw; spilled him out of it, as he leaned to the push; and so he fell flat-faced upon the sea.

Ripplingly withdrawing from his prey, Moby Dick now lay at a little distance, vertically thrusting his oblong white head up and down in the billows; and at the same time slowly revolving his whole spindled body; so that when his vast wrinkled forehead rose—some twenty or more feet out of the water—the now rising swells, with all their confluent waves, dazzlingly broke against it; vindictively tossing their shivered spray still higher into the air.* So, in a gale, the but half baffled Channel billows only recoil from the base of the Eddystone, triumphantly to overleap its summit with their scud.

*This motion is peculiar to the sperm whale. It receives its designation (pitchpoling) from its being likened to that preliminary up-and-down poise of the whale-lance, in the exercise called pitchpoling, previously described. By this motion the whale must best and most comprehensively view whatever objects may be encircling him.

But soon resuming his horizontal attitude, Moby Dick swam swiftly round and round the wrecked crew; sideways churning the water in his vengeful wake, as if lashing himself up to still another and more deadly assault. The sight of the splintered boat seemed to madden him, as the blood of grapes and mulberries cast before Antiochus’s elephants in the book of Maccabees. Meanwhile Ahab half smothered in the foam of the whale’s insolent tail, and too much of a cripple to swim,—though he could still keep afloat, even in the heart of such a whirlpool as that; helpless Ahab’s head was seen, like a tossed bubble which the least chance shock might burst. From the boat’s fragmentary stern, Fedallah incuriously and mildly eyed him; the clinging crew, at the other drifting end, could not succor him; more than enough was it for them to look to themselves. For so revolvingly appalling was the White Whale’s aspect, and so planetarily swift the ever-contracting circles he made, that he seemed horizontally swooping upon them. And though the other boats, unharmed, still hovered hard by; still they dared not pull into the eddy to strike, lest that should be the signal for the instant destruction of the jeopardized castaways, Ahab and all; nor in that case could they themselves hope to escape. With straining eyes, then, they remained on the outer edge of the direful zone, whose centre had now become the old man’s head.

Meantime, from the beginning all this had been descried from the ship’s mast heads; and squaring her yards, she had borne down upon the scene; and was now so nigh, that Ahab in the water hailed her!—“Sail on the”—but that moment a breaking sea dashed on him from Moby Dick, and whelmed him for the time. But struggling out of it again, and chancing to rise on a towering crest, he shouted,—“Sail on the whale!—Drive him off!”
The Pequod’s prows were pointed; and breaking up the charmed circle, she effectually parted the white whale from his victim. As he sullenly swam off, the boats flew to the rescue.

Dragged into Stubb’s boat with blood-shot, blinded eyes, the white brine caking in his wrinkles; the long tension of Ahab’s bodily strength did crack, and helplessly he yielded to his body’s doom: for a time, lying all crushed in the bottom of Stubb’s boat, like one trodden under foot of herds of elephants. Far inland, nameless wails came from him, as desolate sounds from out ravines.

But this intensity of his physical prostration did but so much the more abbreviate it. In an instant’s compass, great hearts sometimes condense to one deep pang, the sum total of those shallow pains kindly diffused through feebler men’s whole lives. And so, such hearts, though summary in each one suffering; still, if the gods decree it, in their life-time aggregate a whole age of woe, wholly made up of instantaneous intensities; for even in their pointless centres, those noble natures contain the entire circumferences of inferior souls.
“The harpoon,” said Ahab, half way rising, and draggingly leaning on one bended arm—“is it safe?”
“Aye, sir, for it was not darted; this is it,” said Stubb, showing it.
“Lay it before me;—any missing men?”
“One, two, three, four, five;—there were five oars, sir, and here are five men.”

“That’s good.—Help me, man; I wish to stand. So, so, I see him! there! there! going to leeward still; what a leaping spout!—Hands off from me! The eternal sap runs up in Ahab’s bones again! Set the sail; out oars; the helm!”

It is often the case that when a boat is stove, its crew, being picked up by another boat, help to work that second boat; and the chase is thus continued with what is called double-banked oars. It was thus now. But the added power of the boat did not equal the added power of the whale, for he seemed to have treble-banked his every fin; swimming with a velocity which plainly showed, that if now, under these circumstances, pushed on, the chase would prove an indefinitely prolonged, if not a hopeless one; nor could any crew endure for so long a period, such an unintermitted, intense straining at the oar; a thing barely tolerable only in some one brief vicissitude. The ship itself, then, as it sometimes happens, offered the most promising intermediate means of overtaking the chase. Accordingly, the boats now made for her, and were soon swayed up to their cranes—the two parts of the wrecked boat having been previously secured by her—and then hoisting everything to her side, and stacking her canvas high up, and sideways outstretching it with stun-sails, like the double-jointed wings of an albatross; the Pequod bore down in the leeward wake of Moby-Dick. At the well known, methodic intervals, the whale’s glittering spout was regularly announced from the manned mast-heads; and when he would be reported as just gone down, Ahab would take the time, and then pacing the deck, binnacle-watch in hand, so soon as the last second of the allotted hour expired, his voice was heard.—“Whose is the doubloon now? D’ye see him?” and if the reply was, No, sir! straightway he commanded them to lift him to his perch. In this way the day wore on; Ahab, now aloft and motionless; anon, unrestingly pacing the planks.

As he was thus walking, uttering no sound, except to hail the men aloft, or to bid them hoist a sail still higher, or to spread one to a still greater breadth—thus to and fro pacing, beneath his slouched hat, at every turn he passed his own wrecked boat, which had been dropped upon the quarter-deck, and lay there reversed; broken bow to shattered stern. At last he paused before it; and as in an already over-clouded sky fresh troops of clouds will sometimes sail across, so over the old man’s face there now stole some such added gloom as this.

Stubb saw him pause; and perhaps intending, not vainly, though, to evince his own unabated fortitude, and thus keep up a valiant place in his Captain’s mind, he advanced, and eyeing the wreck exclaimed—“The thistle the ass refused; it pricked his mouth too keenly, sir; ha! ha!”

“What soulless thing is this that laughs before a wreck? Man, man! did I not know thee brave as fearless fire (and as mechanical) I could swear thou wert a poltroon. Groan nor laugh should be heard before a wreck.”
“Aye, sir,” said Starbuck drawing near, “’tis a solemn sight; an omen, and an ill one.”

“Omen? omen?—the dictionary! If the gods think to speak outright to man, they will honorably speak outright; not shake their heads, and give an old wives’ darkling hint.—Begone! Ye two are the opposite poles of one thing; Starbuck is Stubb reversed, and Stubb is Starbuck; and ye two are all mankind; and Ahab stands alone among the millions of the peopled earth, nor gods nor men his neighbors! Cold, cold—I shiver!—How now? Aloft there! D’ye see him? Sing out for every spout, though he spout ten times a second!”
The day was nearly done; only the hem of his golden robe was rustling. Soon, it was almost dark, but the look-out men still remained unset.
“Can’t see the spout now, sir;—too dark”—cried a voice from the air.
“How heading when last seen?”
“As before, sir,—straight to leeward.”

“Good! he will travel slower now ’tis night. Down royals and top-gallant stun-sails, Mr. Starbuck. We must not run over him before morning; he’s making a passage now, and may heave-to a while. Helm there! keep her full before the wind!—Aloft! come down!—Mr. Stubb, send a fresh hand to the fore-mast head, and see it manned till morning.”—Then advancing towards the doubloon in the main-mast—“Men, this gold is mine, for I earned it; but I shall let it abide here till the White Whale is dead; and then, whosoever of ye first raises him, upon the day he shall be killed, this gold is that man’s; and if on that day I shall again raise him, then, ten times its sum shall be divided among all of ye! Away now!—the deck is thine, sir!”
And so saying, he placed himself half way within the scuttle, and slouching his hat, stood there till dawn, except when at intervals rousing himself to see how the night wore on.

But only slipping further into the whale’s mouth, and tilting over sideways as it slipped, the boat had shaken off his hold on the jaw; spilled him out of it, as he leaned to the push; and so he fell flat-faced upon the sea.

Ripplingly withdrawing from his prey, Moby Dick now lay at a little distance, vertically thrusting his oblong white head up and down in the billows; and at the same time slowly revolving his whole spindled body; so that when his vast wrinkled forehead rose—some twenty or more feet out of the water—the now rising swells, with all their confluent waves, dazzlingly broke against it; vindictively tossing their shivered spray still higher into the air.* So, in a gale, the but half baffled Channel billows only recoil from the base of the Eddystone, triumphantly to overleap its summit with their scud.

*This motion is peculiar to the sperm whale. It receives its designation (pitchpoling) from its being likened to that preliminary up-and-down poise of the whale-lance, in the exercise called pitchpoling, previously described. By this motion the whale must best and most comprehensively view whatever objects may be encircling him.

But soon resuming his horizontal attitude, Moby Dick swam swiftly round and round the wrecked crew; sideways churning the water in his vengeful wake, as if lashing himself up to still another and more deadly assault. The sight of the splintered boat seemed to madden him, as the blood of grapes and mulberries cast before Antiochus’s elephants in the book of Maccabees. Meanwhile Ahab half smothered in the foam of the whale’s insolent tail, and too much of a cripple to swim,—though he could still keep afloat, even in the heart of such a whirlpool as that; helpless Ahab’s head was seen, like a tossed bubble which the least chance shock might burst. From the boat’s fragmentary stern, Fedallah incuriously and mildly eyed him; the clinging crew, at the other drifting end, could not succor him; more than enough was it for them to look to themselves. For so revolvingly appalling was the White Whale’s aspect, and so planetarily swift the ever-contracting circles he made, that he seemed horizontally swooping upon them. And though the other boats, unharmed, still hovered hard by; still they dared not pull into the eddy to strike, lest that should be the signal for the instant destruction of the jeopardized castaways, Ahab and all; nor in that case could they themselves hope to escape. With straining eyes, then, they remained on the outer edge of the direful zone, whose centre had now become the old man’s head.

Meantime, from the beginning all this had been descried from the ship’s mast heads; and squaring her yards, she had borne down upon the scene; and was now so nigh, that Ahab in the water hailed her!—“Sail on the”—but that moment a breaking sea dashed on him from Moby Dick, and whelmed him for the time. But struggling out of it again, and chancing to rise on a towering crest, he shouted,—“Sail on the whale!—Drive him off!”
The Pequod’s prows were pointed; and breaking up the charmed circle, she effectually parted the white whale from his victim. As he sullenly swam off, the boats flew to the rescue.

Dragged into Stubb’s boat with blood-shot, blinded eyes, the white brine caking in his wrinkles; the long tension of Ahab’s bodily strength did crack, and helplessly he yielded to his body’s doom: for a time, lying all crushed in the bottom of Stubb’s boat, like one trodden under foot of herds of elephants. Far inland, nameless wails came from him, as desolate sounds from out ravines.

But this intensity of his physical prostration did but so much the more abbreviate it. In an instant’s compass, great hearts sometimes condense to one deep pang, the sum total of those shallow pains kindly diffused through feebler men’s whole lives. And so, such hearts, though summary in each one suffering; still, if the gods decree it, in their life-time aggregate a whole age of woe, wholly made up of instantaneous intensities; for even in their pointless centres, those noble natures contain the entire circumferences of inferior souls.
“The harpoon,” said Ahab, half way rising, and draggingly leaning on one bended arm—“is it safe?”
“Aye, sir, for it was not darted; this is it,” said Stubb, showing it.
“Lay it before me;—any missing men?”
“One, two, three, four, five;—there were five oars, sir, and here are five men.”

“That’s good.—Help me, man; I wish to stand. So, so, I see him! there! there! going to leeward still; what a leaping spout!—Hands off from me! The eternal sap runs up in Ahab’s bones again! Set the sail; out oars; the helm!”

It is often the case that when a boat is stove, its crew, being picked up by another boat, help to work that second boat; and the chase is thus continued with what is called double-banked oars. It was thus now. But the added power of the boat did not equal the added power of the whale, for he seemed to have treble-banked his every fin; swimming with a velocity which plainly showed, that if now, under these circumstances, pushed on, the chase would prove an indefinitely prolonged, if not a hopeless one; nor could any crew endure for so long a period, such an unintermitted, intense straining at the oar; a thing barely tolerable only in some one brief vicissitude. The ship itself, then, as it sometimes happens, offered the most promising intermediate means of overtaking the chase. Accordingly, the boats now made for her, and were soon swayed up to their cranes—the two parts of the wrecked boat having been previously secured by her—and then hoisting everything to her side, and stacking her canvas high up, and sideways outstretching it with stun-sails, like the double-jointed wings of an albatross; the Pequod bore down in the leeward wake of Moby-Dick. At the well known, methodic intervals, the whale’s glittering spout was regularly announced from the manned mast-heads; and when he would be reported as just gone down, Ahab would take the time, and then pacing the deck, binnacle-watch in hand, so soon as the last second of the allotted hour expired, his voice was heard.—“Whose is the doubloon now? D’ye see him?” and if the reply was, No, sir! straightway he commanded them to lift him to his perch. In this way the day wore on; Ahab, now aloft and motionless; anon, unrestingly pacing the planks.

As he was thus walking, uttering no sound, except to hail the men aloft, or to bid them hoist a sail still higher, or to spread one to a still greater breadth—thus to and fro pacing, beneath his slouched hat, at every turn he passed his own wrecked boat, which had been dropped upon the quarter-deck, and lay there reversed; broken bow to shattered stern. At last he paused before it; and as in an already over-clouded sky fresh troops of clouds will sometimes sail across, so over the old man’s face there now stole some such added gloom as this.

Stubb saw him pause; and perhaps intending, not vainly, though, to evince his own unabated fortitude, and thus keep up a valiant place in his Captain’s mind, he advanced, and eyeing the wreck exclaimed—“The thistle the ass refused; it pricked his mouth too keenly, sir; ha! ha!”

“What soulless thing is this that laughs before a wreck? Man, man! did I not know thee brave as fearless fire (and as mechanical) I could swear thou wert a poltroon. Groan nor laugh should be heard before a wreck.”
“Aye, sir,” said Starbuck drawing near, “’tis a solemn sight; an omen, and an ill one.”

“Omen? omen?—the dictionary! If the gods think to speak outright to man, they will honorably speak outright; not shake their heads, and give an old wives’ darkling hint.—Begone! Ye two are the opposite poles of one thing; Starbuck is Stubb reversed, and Stubb is Starbuck; and ye two are all mankind; and Ahab stands alone among the millions of the peopled earth, nor gods nor men his neighbors! Cold, cold—I shiver!—How now? Aloft there! D’ye see him? Sing out for every spout, though he spout ten times a second!”
The day was nearly done; only the hem of his golden robe was rustling. Soon, it was almost dark, but the look-out men still remained unset.
“Can’t see the spout now, sir;—too dark”—cried a voice from the air.
“How heading when last seen?”
“As before, sir,—straight to leeward.”

“Good! he will travel slower now ’tis night. Down royals and top-gallant stun-sails, Mr. Starbuck. We must not run over him before morning; he’s making a passage now, and may heave-to a while. Helm there! keep her full before the wind!—Aloft! come down!—Mr. Stubb, send a fresh hand to the fore-mast head, and see it manned till morning.”—Then advancing towards the doubloon in the main-mast—“Men, this gold is mine, for I earned it; but I shall let it abide here till the White Whale is dead; and then, whosoever of ye first raises him, upon the day he shall be killed, this gold is that man’s; and if on that day I shall again raise him, then, ten times its sum shall be divided among all of ye! Away now!—the deck is thine, sir!”
And so saying, he placed himself half way within the scuttle, and slouching his hat, stood there till dawn, except when at intervals rousing himself to see how the night wore on.

modern_en.title: Chapter 133 — The Chase—First Day
paragraphs: That night, during the middle watch, when the old man — as he did from time to time — stepped out of the scuttle where he had been leaning and went to his pivot-hole, he suddenly thrust his face out fiercely and sniffed the sea air, the way a clever ship's dog will when the ship draws near some savage island. He declared that a whale must be close. Soon the whole watch could smell that peculiar odor which the living sperm whale sometimes gives off to a great distance; and no sailor was surprised when Ahab, after checking the compass, then the dog-vane, and then fixing the exact bearing of the smell as nearly as he could, quickly ordered the ship's course altered slightly and the sail shortened.

The shrewd thinking behind these movements was sufficiently proved at daybreak by the sight of a long slick on the sea directly and lengthwise ahead, smooth as oil, and resembling, in the pleated watery wrinkles bordering it, the polished metallic marks of some swift tidal rip at the mouth of a deep, rapid stream.
"Man the mastheads! Call all hands!"

Thundering on the forecastle deck with the butts of three clubbed handspikes, Daggoo woke the sleepers with such Judgment-Day claps that they seemed to be breathed out of the scuttle, so instantly did they appear, clothes in hand.
"What do you see?" cried Ahab, flattening his face to the sky.
"Nothing, nothing, sir!" was the sound hailing down in reply.
"Topgallant sails! Stunsails! Aloft and alow, and on both sides!"

All sail being set, he now cast loose the life-line, reserved for swaying him up to the main royal-masthead; and in a few moments they were hoisting him there. He was only two-thirds of the way aloft, peering ahead through the horizontal vacancy between the main-topsail and topgallant-sail, when he raised a gull-like cry in the air. "There she blows! — there she blows! A hump like a snow-hill! It is Moby Dick!"

Fired by the cry, which the three lookouts seemed to take up at the same moment, the men on deck rushed into the rigging to see the famous whale they had been pursuing so long. Ahab had now reached his final perch, some feet above the other lookouts, with Tashtego standing just below him on the cap of the topgallant-mast, so that the Indian's head was almost level with Ahab's heel. From this height the whale could now be seen a mile or so ahead, showing his high, sparkling hump at every roll of the sea and regularly jetting his silent spout into the air. To the credulous sailors it seemed the same silent spout they had seen so long ago in the moonlit Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
"And did none of you see it before?" cried Ahab, hailing the perched men all around him.
"I saw him almost that same instant, sir, that Captain Ahab did, and I cried out," said Tashtego.

"Not the same instant; not the same — no, the doubloon is mine; Fate kept the doubloon for me. Only I; none of you could have raised the White Whale first. There she blows! — there she blows! — there she blows! There again! — there again!" he cried, in long-drawn, lingering, measured tones, keeping time with the gradual lengthening of the whale's visible jets. "He's going to sound! In stunsails! Down topgallant-sails! Stand by three boats. Mr. Starbuck, remember, stay on board and keep the ship. Helm there! Luff, luff a point! So; steady, man, steady! There go flukes! No, no; only black water! All ready the boats there? Stand by, stand by! Lower me, Mr. Starbuck; lower, lower — quick, quicker!" And he slid through the air to the deck.
"He is heading straight to leeward, sir," cried Stubb, "right away from us; cannot have seen the ship yet."
"Be quiet, man! Stand by the braces! Hard down the helm! — brace up! Shiver her! — shiver her! So; well that! Boats, boats!"

Soon all the boats except Starbuck's were lowered; all the boat-sails were set and all the paddles working, and they shot to leeward with rippling speed, Ahab leading the charge. A pale, deathly glimmer lit up Fedallah's sunken eyes; a hideous movement gnawed at his mouth.

Like noiseless nautilus shells, their light prows sped through the sea; but they closed on the foe only slowly. As they came nearer, the ocean grew smoother still; it seemed to be drawing a carpet over its waves; it seemed a noon meadow, so serenely did it spread. At length the breathless hunter came so close to his seemingly unsuspecting prey that the whale's entire dazzling hump was plainly visible, sliding along the sea as if it were a thing apart, and ringed all the while by a revolving circle of the finest, fleecy, greenish foam. Beyond it he saw the vast, intricate wrinkles of the slightly projecting head. Ahead of the whale, far out on the soft waters patterned like a Turkish rug, went the glistening white shadow of his broad, milky forehead, with a musical rippling playfully keeping the shadow company; behind, the blue waters flowed in turn into the moving valley of his steady wake; and on either side bright bubbles rose and danced along beside him. But these were broken again by the light toes of hundreds of gay sea-birds softly feathering the sea between their fitful flights; and like some flagstaff rising from the painted hull of an argosy, the tall but shattered pole of a recent lance stuck up from the white whale's back; and every so often one of the cloud of soft-toed birds, hovering and skimming to and fro like a canopy over the fish, would silently perch and rock on this pole, its long tail feathers streaming like pennons.

A gentle joyousness — a mighty mildness of repose in swiftness — clothed the gliding whale. Not the white bull Jupiter, swimming away with the ravished Europa clinging to his graceful horns, his lovely, leering eyes turned sideways on the girl, rippling with smooth, bewitching speed straight for the bridal bower in Crete — not Jove, not that great majesty Supreme! — surpassed the glorified White Whale as he swam so divinely.

On each soft side — in step with the parted swell that, once it left him, flowed so far and wide away — on each bright side, the whale gave off enticements. No wonder there had been some among the hunters who, carried away and allured beyond words by all this serenity, had ventured to attack it, only to find, fatally, that this quietude was nothing but the garment of tornadoes. Yet calm, enticing calm, oh whale! You glide on before all who see you for the first time, no matter how many in that same way you may have tricked and destroyed before.

And so, through the calm serenity of the tropical sea, among waves whose hand-clapping was held back by overwhelming rapture, Moby Dick moved on, still keeping the full terrors of his submerged trunk out of sight and completely hiding the twisted hideousness of his jaw. But soon the front of him slowly rose out of the water; for an instant his whole marble-like body formed a high arch, like Virginia's Natural Bridge; and, waving his bannered flukes in the air in warning, the grand god revealed himself, sounded, and disappeared. Hovering, pausing and dipping on the wing, the white seabirds lingered longingly over the churning pool he left behind.
With oars peaked, blades raised clear of the water, and paddles down, the sheets of their sails adrift, the three boats now silently floated, awaiting Moby Dick's reappearance.

"An hour," said Ahab, standing rooted in the stern of his boat; and he gazed past the place where the whale had been, toward the dim blue spaces and wide, wooing emptiness to leeward. It lasted only an instant; for his eyes again seemed to whirl around in his head as he swept the circle of water. The breeze was freshening now; the sea began to swell.
"The birds! — the birds!" cried Tashtego.

In long Indian file, like herons taking wing, the white birds were now all flying toward Ahab's boat; and when they were within a few yards they began fluttering over the water there, wheeling round and round with joyous, expectant cries. Their vision was keener than man's; Ahab could find no sign in the sea. But suddenly, as he peered down and down into its depths, far down he saw a white living spot no bigger than a white weasel rising with wonderful speed and growing larger as it rose, until it turned, and then two long crooked rows of white, glistening teeth were plainly revealed, floating up from the unfathomable bottom. It was Moby Dick's open mouth and scrolled jaw, his vast, shadowed bulk still half blending with the blue of the sea. The glittering mouth yawned beneath the boat like a marble tomb with its door open; and with one sidelong sweep of his steering oar, Ahab whirled the boat aside from this tremendous apparition. Then, calling on Fedallah to change places with him, he went forward to the bow, seized Perth's harpoon, and ordered his crew to grip their oars and stand ready to back the boat astern.

Now, because the boat had been spun round on its axis in time, its bow was made to face the whale's head in advance, while the head was still under water. But as if he saw through this stratagem, Moby Dick, with that malicious intelligence ascribed to him, shifted himself sideways in an instant, as it were, shooting his pleated head lengthwise beneath the boat.

Through and through — through every plank and every rib — a thrill ran for an instant, as the whale, lying obliquely on his back in the manner of a biting shark, slowly and sensitively took the bows fully into his mouth, so that the long, narrow, scrolled lower jaw curled high up into the open air, and one of the teeth caught in a rowlock. The bluish pearl-white of the inside of the jaw was within six inches of Ahab's head, and reached higher than that. In this position the White Whale now shook the slight cedar boat as a mildly cruel cat shakes her mouse. Fedallah gazed with unastonished eyes and crossed his arms; but the tiger-yellow crew were tumbling over each other's heads to reach the farthest end of the stern.

And now the two springy gunwales were bending in and out as the whale toyed with the doomed boat in this devilish way; his body was submerged beneath the boat, so he could not be darted at from the bow, for the bow was almost inside him, as it were; and the other boats had involuntarily paused, as before a sudden crisis impossible to withstand. It was then that the monomaniac Ahab, furious at being so tantalizingly close to his foe — a closeness that put him, fully alive and helpless, in the very jaws he hated — frenzied by all this, seized the long bone with his bare hands and wildly strove to wrench it loose from its grip. As he strove in vain, the jaw slipped from him; the frail gunwales bent in, collapsed, and snapped, as both jaws, like enormous shears, slid further aft, bit the boat completely in two, and locked themselves shut again in the sea, midway between the two floating wrecks. These drifted apart, their broken ends drooping, the crew at the stern-wreck clinging to the gunwales and struggling to hold on to the oars in order to lash them across.

At that opening moment, before the boat was snapped, Ahab had been the first to see the whale's intent, from the crafty lifting of his head — a movement that loosened his hold for the time — and at that moment his hand made one final effort to push the boat out of the bite. But the boat, only slipping further into the whale's mouth and tilting sideways as it slipped, had shaken off his hold on the jaw and spilled him out as he leaned into the push; and so he fell flat on his face upon the sea.

Rippling away from his prey, Moby Dick now lay a little distance off, thrusting his oblong white head vertically up and down in the billows while slowly revolving his whole spindle-shaped body; so that whenever his vast wrinkled forehead rose — some twenty feet or more out of the water — the swells, now rising, broke dazzlingly against it with all their merging waves, vindictively tossing their shattered spray still higher into the air.* So, in a gale, the Channel billows, only half baffled, recoil from the base of the Eddystone lighthouse only to leap triumphantly over its summit with their scud.

*This motion is peculiar to the sperm whale. It gets its name (pitchpoling) because it is likened to the preliminary up-and-down poise of the whale-lance in the exercise called pitchpoling, described earlier. By this motion the whale must best and most comprehensively view whatever objects may be encircling him.

But soon, returning to a horizontal position, Moby Dick swam swiftly round and round the wrecked crew, churning the water sideways in his vengeful wake, as if whipping himself up to yet another and deadlier attack. The sight of the splintered boat seemed to madden him, as the blood of grapes and mulberries, cast before Antiochus's elephants in the book of Maccabees, maddened them. Meanwhile Ahab was half smothered in the foam of the whale's insolent tail, and too much of a cripple to swim — though he could still keep afloat, even in the heart of a whirlpool like that — and helpless Ahab's head could be seen like a tossed bubble that the slightest chance shock might burst. From the broken-off stern of the boat Fedallah watched him with mild indifference; the clinging crew at the other drifting end could not help him; it was more than enough for them to look after themselves. For the White Whale's aspect as he revolved was so appalling, and the ever-tightening circles he made were so swift, like a planet's, that he seemed to be swooping horizontally upon them. And though the other boats, unharmed, still hovered close by, they dared not pull into the eddy to strike, for fear that would be the signal for the instant destruction of the endangered castaways, Ahab and all; nor in that case could they themselves hope to escape. So, with straining eyes, they stayed on the outer edge of the dreadful zone, whose center had now become the old man's head.

Meanwhile, from the beginning all this had been seen from the ship's mastheads; and squaring her yards, she had borne down upon the scene; and was now so near that Ahab in the water hailed her! "Sail on the" — but that moment a breaking sea dashed on him from Moby Dick, and overwhelmed him for the time. But struggling out of it again, and chancing to rise on a towering crest, he shouted: "Sail on the whale! Drive him off!"
The Pequod's bows were pointed at them; breaking up the charmed circle, she succeeded in separating the white whale from his victim. As he swam sullenly away, the boats flew to the rescue.

Ahab was dragged into Stubb's boat with bloodshot, blinded eyes, the white brine caking in his wrinkles; and the long tension of his bodily strength cracked, and helplessly he yielded to his body's doom: for a time, lying all crushed in the bottom of Stubb's boat, like one trodden underfoot by herds of elephants. Far inland, nameless wails came from him, like desolate sounds from out of ravines.

But the very intensity of his physical collapse only made it the shorter. Within the span of an instant, great hearts sometimes condense into one deep pang the sum total of those shallow pains that are mercifully spread through the whole lives of feebler men. And so such hearts, though brief in each single suffering, still, if the gods decree it, pile up in their lifetime a whole age of woe, made up entirely of instantaneous intensities; for even in their centers, mere points though these are, those noble natures contain the entire circumferences of inferior souls.
"The harpoon," said Ahab, half-rising and draggingly leaning on one bent arm — "is it safe?"
"Aye, sir, for it was not darted; this is it," said Stubb, showing it.
"Lay it before me; any missing men?"
"One, two, three, four, five; there were five oars, sir, and here are five men."

"That's good. Help me, man; I wish to stand. So, so, I see him! There! There! Going to leeward still; what a leaping spout! — Hands off from me! The eternal sap runs up in Ahab's bones again! Set the sail; out oars; the helm!"

It often happens that when a boat is stove, its crew, once picked up by another boat, help to work that second boat; and the chase is then continued with what are called double-banked oars. So it was now. But the added power of the boat did not match the added power of the whale, for he seemed to have treble-banked every fin, swimming at a speed that plainly showed that if the chase were pushed on now, under these circumstances, it would prove an indefinitely prolonged one, if not a hopeless one; nor could any crew endure such unbroken, intense straining at the oar for so long a period — a thing barely bearable even for one brief spell. The ship itself, then, as sometimes happens, offered the most promising way of overtaking the chase in the meantime. Accordingly, the boats now made for her and were soon swayed up to their cranes — the two parts of the wrecked boat having already been secured by her — and then, hoisting everything up to her side, piling her canvas high, and stretching it out sideways with stunsails like the double-jointed wings of an albatross, the Pequod bore down in Moby Dick's leeward wake. At the familiar, regular intervals, the whale's glittering spout was duly announced from the manned mastheads; and whenever he was reported as just gone down, Ahab would note the time, and then, pacing the deck binnacle-watch in hand, the moment the last second of the allotted hour ran out, his voice was heard: "Whose is the doubloon now? Do you see him?" And if the reply was "No, sir!" he at once ordered them to hoist him to his perch. In this way the day wore on; Ahab now aloft and motionless, now pacing the planks without rest.

As he walked like this, making no sound except to hail the men aloft or to tell them to hoist a sail still higher or spread one still wider — pacing back and forth like this beneath his slouched hat — at every turn he passed his own wrecked boat, which had been dropped onto the quarter-deck and lay there upside down, broken bow to shattered stern. At last he stopped in front of it; and just as fresh troops of clouds will sometimes sail across a sky that is already overcast, so some such added gloom now crept over the old man's face.

Stubb saw him stop; and perhaps meaning — though not vainly — to show that his own courage was undiminished, and so keep a brave place in his Captain's thoughts, he stepped forward and, eyeing the wreck, exclaimed, "The thistle the ass refused; it pricked his mouth too sharply, sir; ha! ha!"

"What soulless thing is this that laughs in front of a wreck? Man, man! If I did not know you to be as brave as fearless fire (and as mechanical), I could swear you were a coward. Neither groan nor laugh should be heard in front of a wreck."
"Aye, sir," said Starbuck, drawing near, "it is a solemn sight; an omen, and an ill one."

"Omen? Omen? — the dictionary! If the gods mean to speak outright to man, they will honorably speak outright; not shake their heads and give an old wives' dark hint. — Begone! You two are the opposite poles of one thing; Starbuck is Stubb reversed, and Stubb is Starbuck; and you two are all mankind; and Ahab stands alone among the millions of the peopled earth, with neither gods nor men for his neighbors! Cold, cold — I shiver! — What now? Aloft there! Do you see him? Sing out for every spout, even if he spouts ten times a second!"
The day was nearly done; only the hem of its golden robe was rustling. Soon it was almost dark, but the lookout men still remained at their posts.
"Can't see the spout now, sir; too dark," cried a voice from the air.
"How heading when last seen?"
"As before, sir — straight to leeward."

"Good! He will travel slower now that it's night. Down royals and topgallant stunsails, Mr. Starbuck. We must not run over him before morning; he's making a passage now, and may heave to for a while. Helm there! Keep her full before the wind! — Aloft! Come down! — Mr. Stubb, send a fresh hand to the fore-masthead, and see that it's manned till morning." Then, advancing toward the doubloon on the mainmast: "Men, this gold is mine, for I earned it; but I shall let it stay here till the White Whale is dead; and then, whichever of you first raises him on the day he is killed, this gold is that man's; and if on that day I raise him again myself, then ten times its sum shall be divided among all of you! Away now! — the deck is yours, sir!"
Saying this, he stationed himself halfway inside the scuttle, pulled his hat down low, and stood there until dawn, except when he roused himself now and then to see how the night was going.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 133 — Jagten — Første dag
paragraphs: Den nat, i midtervagten, trådte den gamle mand — som han fra tid til anden gjorde — ud af lugen, hvor han havde stået og lænet sig, og hen til sit drejehul. Pludselig stak han ansigtet voldsomt frem og snusede til havluften, som en klog skibshund gør, når skibet nærmer sig en vild ø. Han erklærede, at en hval måtte være tæt på. Snart kunne hele vagten lugte den ejendommelige lugt, som den levende kaskelot nogle gange afgiver på stor afstand; og ingen sømand var forbavset, da Ahab, efter at have set på kompasset, så på vindhanen og derefter fastlagt lugtens præcise retning så godt, han kunne, hurtigt beordrede skibets kurs ændret en smule og sejlene kortet.

Den kloge tanke bag disse bevægelser blev ved daggry tilstrækkeligt bevist ved synet af en lang glat stribe på havet lige forude i skibets længderetning. Den var glat som olie, og med de rynkede vandfolder langs kanten lignede den de polerede, metalagtige mærker fra en hurtig tidevandsstrøm ved udmundingen af en dyb, strid flod.
»Bemand mastetoppene! Kald alle mand!«

Daggoo dundrede på forkastellets dæk med enderne af tre sammenknyttede spage og vækkede de sovende med sådanne dommedagsbulder, at de syntes at blive pustet op af lugen, så hurtigt dukkede de op med tøjet i hånden.
»Hvad ser I?« råbte Ahab og vendte ansigtet fladt mod himlen.
»Intet, intet, sir!« lød det ned som svar.
»Bramsejl! Studsejl! Oppe og nede, og på begge sider!«

Da alle sejl var sat, løste han nu livlinen, der var forbeholdt til at svinge ham op til stormastens bramstang, og et øjeblik efter hejste de ham derop. Han var kun to tredjedele af vejen op og spejdede forud gennem det vandrette mellemrum mellem stormarssejlet og bramsejlet, da han udstødte et mågeagtigt skrig i luften: »Der blæser hun! — der blæser hun! En pukkel som en snebakke! Det er Moby Dick!«

Tændt af råbet, som de tre udkigsmænd syntes at tage op i samme øjeblik, styrtede mændene på dækket op i takkelagen for at se den berømte hval, de så længe havde forfulgt. Ahab var nu nået til sin sidste siddeplads, nogle fod over de andre udkigsmænd, mens Tashtego stod lige under ham på bramstangens knop, så indianerens hoved næsten var i højde med Ahabs hæl. Fra denne højde kunne hvalen nu ses omkring en engelsk mil forude, hvor den ved hver rulning i havet viste sin høje, glitrende pukkel og med jævne mellemrum sendte sin lydløse stråle op i luften. For de godtroende sømænd lignede det den samme lydløse stråle, de for så længe siden havde set i det måneoplyste Atlanterhav og Det Indiske Ocean.
»Og var der ingen af jer, der så den før?« råbte Ahab og kaldte på de mænd, der sad rundt om ham.
»Jeg så ham næsten i samme øjeblik, sir, som kaptajn Ahab gjorde, og jeg råbte,« sagde Tashtego.

»Ikke samme øjeblik; ikke samme — nej, dublonen er min; skæbnen holdt dublonen tilbage til mig. Kun jeg; ingen af jer kunne have set den hvide hval først. Der blæser hun! — der blæser hun! — der blæser hun! Der igen! — der igen!« råbte han med lange, trækkende, afmålte toner i takt med, at hvalens synlige sprøjt gradvis blev længere. »Den går ned! Ind med studsejlene! Ned med bramsejlene! Gør tre både klar. Mr. Starbuck, husk, du bliver om bord og passer skibet. Rorgænger! Luv, luv en streg! Sådan; hold den, mand, hold den! Der går halen! Nej, nej; kun sort vand! Er alle både klar derude? Pas på, pas på! Firer mig ned, Mr. Starbuck; firer, firer — hurtigt, hurtigere!« Og han gled gennem luften ned til dækket.
»Den går lige til læ, sir,« råbte Stubb, »lige væk fra os; kan ikke have set skibet endnu.«
»Hold din mund, mand! Stå klar ved brasserne! Hårdt ned med roret! — brasse op! Lad hende ryste! — lad hende ryste! Sådan; godt det! Både, både!«

Snart var alle både undtagen Starbucks sænket; alle bådenes sejl var sat og alle pagajer i gang, og de skød til læ med sildrende fart, med Ahab i spidsen for angrebet. Et blegt, dødsagtigt skær lyste op i Fedallahs indsunkne øjne; en hæslig bevægelse gnavede i hans mund.

Som lydløse nautilusskaller gled deres lette stævne gennem havet, men de nærmede sig kun langsomt deres fjende. Jo tættere de kom, desto glattere blev havet; det var, som om det bredte et tæppe ud over sine bølger; det lignede en eng ved middagstid, så fredfyldt lå det. Til sidst kom den åndeløse jæger så tæt på sit tilsyneladende intetanende bytte, at hvalens hele skinnende pukkel kunne ses tydeligt, mens den gled hen over havet, som var den noget for sig selv, og hele tiden var omkranset af en roterende ring af det fineste, uldne, grønlige skum. Bag den så han det store hoveds vældige, indviklede rynker, der stak en smule frem. Foran hvalen, langt ude på det bløde vand, der var mønstret som et tyrkisk tæppe, gled den glinsende hvide skygge af hans brede, mælkehvide pande, og en musikalsk risling holdt legende skyggen med selskab. Bagved flød det blå vand sammen i den bevægelige dal efter hans jævne kølvand, og på begge sider steg lyse bobler op og dansede med ham. Men dem brød igen de lette tæer fra hundredvis af glade havfugle, som blidt strejfede havet mellem deres springende flugter. Og som en flagstang, der rejser sig fra det malede skrog på et rigt lastet handelsskib, stak den høje, men splintrede stage fra en nylig lanse op fra den hvide hvals ryg. Af og til satte en fugl fra skyen af blødtåede fugle, der svævede og strøg frem og tilbage som en baldakin over fisken, sig lydløst på stagen og vippede på den, mens dens lange halefjer flagrede som vimpler.

En blid glæde — en mægtig mildhed, en ro midt i farten — klædte den glidende hval. Ikke den hvide tyr Jupiter, som svømmede bort med den bortførte Europa klamret til sine yndefulde horn, med sine dejlige, lokkende øjne vendt sidelæns mod pigen, mens han med glat, fortryllende fart gled lige mod brudekamret på Kreta — ikke Jove, ikke den store, højeste majestæt! — overgik den forherligede hvide hval, da han svømmede så guddommeligt.

På hver bløde side — i takt med den delte bølge, som, når den først forlod ham, bredte sig så langt og vidt bort — på hver lys side udsendte hvalen lokkende bud. Det var ikke så underligt, at nogle af jægerne, som var revet med og ubeskriveligt fristet af al denne ro, havde vovet at angribe ham, kun for at opdage, til deres død, at denne stilhed ikke var andet end stormenes klædedragt. Dog, rolig, lokkende ro, o hval! Du glider frem foran alle, der ser dig for første gang, uanset hvor mange du på samme måde har narret og ødelagt før.

Og sådan bevægede Moby Dick sig videre gennem det tropiske havs rolige stilhed, mellem bølger, hvis klapsalver blev holdt tilbage af overvældende henrykkelse. Han skjulte stadig sin neddykkede krops fulde rædsler og holdt sin kæbes fordrejede hæslighed helt skjult. Men snart steg hans forparti langsomt op af vandet; et øjeblik dannede hele hans marmorlignende krop en høj bue som Virginias Natural Bridge; og mens han i advarsel viftede med sine flagagtige halefinner i luften, viste den store gud sig, dykkede og forsvandt. Svævende, standsende og dykkende på vingerne blev de hvide havfugle længselsfuldt over den oprørte pøl, han efterlod.
Med årerne lodret, bladene løftet klar af vandet og pagajerne nede, sejlenes skøder slækket drev de tre både nu lydløst og ventede på, at Moby Dick skulle dukke op igen.

»En time,« sagde Ahab, mens han stod som rodfæstet agter i sin båd. Og han stirrede forbi stedet, hvor hvalen havde været, mod de dunkle blå vidder og den vide, lokkende tomhed til læ. Det varede kun et øjeblik, for hans øjne syntes igen at hvirvle rundt i hovedet, mens han strejfede vandets kreds. Brisen var ved at blive friskere nu; havet begyndte at hæve sig.
»Fuglene! — fuglene!« råbte Tashtego.

I en lang række, indianerrække, som hejrer, der letter, fløj de hvide fugle nu alle mod Ahabs båd. Da de var nogle få yard fra den, begyndte de at flagre over vandet dér og at kredse rundt og rundt med glade, forventningsfulde skrig. Deres syn var skarpere end menneskets; Ahab kunne ikke finde noget tegn i havet. Men pludselig, mens han stirrede ned og ned i dybet, så han langt nede en hvid, levende plet, ikke større end et hvidt væsel, som steg op med forunderlig fart og blev større, efterhånden som den steg, indtil den vendte sig, og så blev to lange, skæve rækker af hvide, glinsende tænder tydeligt synlige, mens de svævede op fra den bundløse bund. Det var Moby Dicks åbne mund og snoede kæbe, hans vældige, skyggefulde krop, der endnu halvt gik i et med havets blå. Den glitrende mund gabede under båden som en marmorgrav med åben dør. Og med et sidelæns slag af sin styreåre vendte Ahab båden bort fra dette uhyggelige syn. Så kaldte han på Fedallah, så de kunne bytte plads, gik frem i stævnen, greb Perths harpun og befalede sine folk at gribe årerne og stå klar til at bakke båden agterud.

Fordi båden i tide var blevet drejet rundt om sin akse, blev dens stævn nu vendt mod hvalens hoved på forhånd, mens hovedet endnu var under vand. Men som om han gennemskuede denne krigslist, flyttede Moby Dick med den ondskabsfulde klogskab, man tilskrev ham, sig på et øjeblik, så at sige, til siden og skød sit foldede hoved på langs ind under båden.

Gennem og gennem — gennem hver planke og hvert spant — løb der et gys et øjeblik, mens hvalen, der lå skråt på ryggen på samme måde som en bidende haj, langsomt og følsomt tog stævnen helt ind i munden, så den lange, smalle, snoede underkæbe krøllede højt op i den åbne luft, og en af tænderne hægtede sig fast i en åregaffel. Den blålige perlehvide inderside af kæben var inden for seks tommer fra Ahabs hoved og rakte højere op end det. I denne stilling rystede den hvide hval nu den spinkle cederbåd, som en mildt grusom kat ryster sin mus. Fedallah så på med uforbavsede øjne og lagde armene over kors, men den tigergule besætning væltede over hinandens hoveder for at nå helt agterud.

Og nu bøjede de to fjedrende ripper sig ind og ud, mens hvalen legede med den dødsdømte båd på denne djævelske måde. Hans krop var under båden, så man kunne ikke kaste efter ham fra stævnen, for stævnen var så at sige næsten inde i ham. De andre både var uvilkårligt standset, som over for en pludselig krise, man umuligt kan modstå. Da var det, at den monomane Ahab, rasende over at være så pinefuldt tæt på sin fjende — en nærhed, der havde sat ham, fuldt levende og hjælpeløs, i selve de kæber, han hadede — og vanvittig af alt dette, greb den lange knogle med bare hænder og forsøgte vildt at rykke den løs af dens greb. Mens han forgæves kæmpede, gled kæben fra ham. De skrøbelige ripper bøjede sig ind, brast og knækkede, mens begge kæber som enorme sakse gled længere agterud, bed båden helt over i to stykker og lukkede sig sammen igen i havet, midt mellem de to flydende vrag. De drev fra hinanden med nedhængende, knækkede ender, og besætningen på det agterste vrag klamrede sig til ripperne og kæmpede for at holde fast på årerne for at surre dem på tværs.

I det første øjeblik, før båden blev knækket, havde Ahab været den første, der så hvalens hensigt, ud fra hans snedige løft af hovedet — en bevægelse, der løsnede hans greb for en tid — og i det øjeblik gjorde hans hånd et sidste forsøg på at skubbe båden ud af bidet. Men båden gled bare længere ind i hvalens mund og vippede sidelæns, mens den gled. Det rystede hans greb om kæben af og kastede ham ud, da han lænede sig ind i skubbet, og så faldt han fladt på ansigtet ned i havet.

Moby Dick gled væk fra sit bytte og lå nu et stykke borte. Han stak sit aflange, hvide hoved lodret op og ned i bølgerne, mens han langsomt drejede hele sin spoleformede krop rundt, så hver gang hans vældige rynkede pande rejste sig — tyve fod eller mere op af vandet — brød de stigende dønninger blændende mod den med alle deres sammenløbende bølger og kastede hævngerrigt deres knuste skum endnu højere op i luften.* Således kaster Kanalens bølger sig i storm, kun halvt afvist, tilbage fra bunden af Eddystone-fyret, bare for at springe sejrrigt hen over dets top med deres skumsprøjt.

*Denne bevægelse er særlig for kaskelothvalen. Den har fået sit navn (pitchpoling) fordi den sammenlignes med hvallansens indledende op-og-ned-balance i øvelsen, der kaldes pitchpoling, og som er beskrevet tidligere. Ved denne bevægelse kan hvalen bedst og mest overskueligt se, hvad der måtte omringe ham.

Men snart vendte Moby Dick tilbage til vandret stilling og svømmede hurtigt rundt og rundt om det forliste mandskab. Han piskede vandet sidelæns op i sit hævngerrige kølvand, som om han piskede sig selv op til endnu et, endnu dødeligere angreb. Synet af den splintrede båd syntes at gøre ham vanvittig, ligesom druers og morbærs blod, der blev kastet for Antiokus' elefanter i Makkabæerbogen, gjorde dem vanvittige. Imens var Ahab halvt kvalt i skummet fra hvalens frække hale og for meget en krøbling til at svømme — selv om han stadig kunne holde sig oven vande, selv midt i en sådan hvirvel — og den hjælpeløse Ahabs hoved kunne ses som en slynget boble, som det mindste tilfældige stød kunne sprænge. Fra den afbrækkede agterende af båden betragtede Fedallah ham med mild ligegyldighed. De klamrende mænd i den anden drivende ende kunne ikke hjælpe ham; det var mere end nok for dem at passe på sig selv. For den hvide hvals udseende, mens han kredsede, var så skrækindjagende, og de stadig snævrere kredse, han drog, var så hurtige som en planets, at han syntes at nærme sig dem i et vandret styrt. Og selv om de andre både, uskadte, stadig svævede tæt ved, turde de ikke ro ind i strømhvirvlen for at harpunere, af frygt for at det ville blive signalet til de nødstedte skibbrudnes øjeblikkelige undergang, Ahab og alle; og så kunne de heller ikke selv håbe at slippe. Så med anspændte øjne holdt de sig på ydersiden af den frygtelige zone, hvis midte nu var blevet den gamles hoved.

I mellemtiden var alt dette fra begyndelsen set fra skibets mastetoppe. Skibet havde brasset sine rær i vinkel og var gået ned mod stedet, og nu var det så nær, at Ahab i vandet kunne anråbe det! »Sejl på —« men i det øjeblik slog en brydende sø fra Moby Dick over ham og overvældede ham for en tid. Men han kæmpede sig ud af den igen, og da han tilfældigvis steg op på en tårnhøj bølgetop, råbte han: »Sejl på hvalen! Jag ham væk!«
Pequods stævn pegede mod dem. Hun brød den fortryllede kreds, og det lykkedes hende at skille den hvide hval fra hans offer. Mens han svømmede mut bort, fløj bådene til undsætning.

Ahab blev trukket op i Stubbs båd med blodsprængte, blændede øjne, mens det hvide saltvand sad som en skorpe i hans rynker. Den lange anspændelse i hans legemskræfter knækkede, og hjælpeløst gav han sig hen til sin krops dom: for en tid lå han helt knust på bunden af Stubbs båd, som en der er trampet ned af elefantflokke. Langt ind i landet kom navnløse klagerop fra ham, som øde lyde fra kløfter.

Men netop styrken i hans legemlige sammenbrud gjorde det kun kortere. I løbet af et øjeblik samler store hjerter somme tider i ét dybt stik summen af de overfladiske smerter, som barmhjertigt er fordelt over hele livet hos svagere mænd. Og således ophober sådanne hjerter, selv om de er korte i hver enkelt lidelse, om guderne bestemmer det, i deres levetid en hel tidsalder af sorg, der udelukkende består af øjeblikkelige intensiteter. For selv i deres centre, der kun er punkter, rummer disse ædle naturer hele omkredsen af ringere sjæle.
»Harpunen,« sagde Ahab, mens han halvt rejste sig og støttede sig tungt på en bøjet arm, »er den i behold?«
»Ja, sir, for den blev ikke kastet. Her er den,« sagde Stubb og viste den frem.
»Læg den foran mig. Mangler der nogen?«
»En, to, tre, fire, fem. Der var fem årer, sir, og her er fem mand.«

»Godt. Hjælp mig, mand. Jeg vil stå. Sådan, sådan, jeg ser ham! Der! Der! Stadig til læ. Sikke en sprællende blæst! — Hænderne væk fra mig! Den evige saft stiger op i Ahabs knogler igen! Sæt sejlet, ud med årerne, roret!«

Det sker ofte, at når en båd er slået læk, hjælper dens besætning, når den er samlet op af en anden båd, med at ro den anden båd, og jagten fortsættes så med det, der kaldes dobbeltbesatte årer. Sådan var det nu. Men bådens ekstra kraft stod ikke mål med hvalens ekstra kraft, for han syntes at have tredoblet hver finne og svømmede med en fart, der tydeligt viste, at hvis jagten blev ført videre nu, under disse omstændigheder, ville den blive uendeligt langvarig, om ikke håbløs. Og ingen besætning kunne holde ud at anstrenge sig så uafbrudt og intenst ved åren så længe — noget, der næsten ikke er til at bære selv i en kort stund. Skibet selv bød derfor, som det somme tider sker, den mest lovende måde at indhente byttet på i mellemtiden. Bådene styrede altså nu mod det og blev snart svunget op til sine davider — de to dele af den knuste båd var allerede blevet sikret af skibet. Så hejste de alt op langs skibssiden, tårnede sejl højt op og strakte dem sidelæns ud med studsejl som albatrossens dobbeltleddede vinger, og Pequod gik ned i Moby Dicks læside kølvand. Med de velkendte, regelmæssige mellemrum blev hvalens glitrende blæst behørigt meldt fra de bemandede mastetoppe, og hver gang han blev meldt som netop gået ned, noterede Ahab tiden. Så gik han op og ned ad dækket med kompashusets ur i hånden, og i det øjeblik det sidste sekund af den fastsatte time var løbet ud, lød hans stemme: »Hvem har dublonen nu? Ser I ham?« Og hvis svaret var »Nej, sir!«, befalede han straks, at man skulle hejse ham op på hans udkigspost. På den måde gik dagen. Nu sad Ahab oppe og urørlig, nu gik han hvileløst op og ned ad dækket.

Han gik rundt på den måde og sagde ikke en lyd, undtagen for at råbe til mændene i vanten eller byde dem hejse et sejl endnu højere eller spile et endnu bredere ud. Han gik frem og tilbage under sin nedtrukne hat, og for hver vending kom han forbi sin egen knuste båd, som var sat ned på agterdækket og lå der med bunden i vejret, fra den brækkede forstavn til det splintrede agterspejl. Til sidst standsede han foran den. Og ligesom friske skyhære nogle gange sejler hen over en himmel, der allerede er overskyet, sådan sneg der sig nu en ekstra mørkhed ind over den gamle mands ansigt.

Stubb så ham standse. Måske ville han — dog uden at prale — vise, at hans eget mod ikke var knækket, og dermed holde en tapper plads i kaptajnens tanker. Han trådte frem, betragtede vraget og udbrød: »Tidslen, som æslet afviste. Den stak ham for hårdt i munden, sir. Ha! ha!«

»Hvad for en sjælløs ting er det, der står og ler foran et vrag? Mand, mand! Hvis jeg ikke vidste, at du var lige så uforfærdet som ild, der intet frygter (og lige så mekanisk), kunne jeg sværge på, at du var en kujon. Hverken stønnen eller latter skal høres foran et vrag.«
»Ja, sir,« sagde Starbuck og kom nærmere, »det er et alvorligt syn. Et varsel, og et ondt et.«

»Varsel? Varsel? Ordbogen! Hvis guderne vil tale lige ud til mennesket, vil de tale lige ud, som det sømmer sig. De vil ikke ryste på hovedet og give et mørkt vink som gamle koner. — Af sted med jer! I to er modsatte poler af én og samme ting. Starbuck er Stubb vendt om, og Stubb er Starbuck, og I to er hele menneskeheden. Og Ahab står alene blandt millionerne på den befolkede jord, uden guder og uden mennesker som naboer! Koldt, koldt — jeg ryster! — Hvad nu? Hallo, deroppe! Ser I ham? Råb op for hver eneste blæsning, selv om han blæser ti gange i sekundet!«
Dagen var næsten forbi. Kun kanten af dens gyldne kåbe raslede endnu. Snart var det næsten mørkt, men udkigsmændene blev stadig på deres poster.
»Kan ikke se blæsten mere, sir. For mørkt,« råbte en stemme fra luften.
»Hvilken kurs havde han, da du sidst så ham?«
»Som før, sir. Lige til læ.«

»Godt! Han svømmer langsommere nu, når det er nat. Ned med royalsejl og bramstudsejl, Mr. Starbuck. Vi må ikke sejle forbi ham før morgen. Han er på en lang strækning nu og lægger måske bi et stykke tid. Roret derovre! Hold hende helt for vinden! — Deroppe! Kom ned! — Mr. Stubb, send en frisk mand op i fokkemasten og sørg for, at der er mand deroppe til morgen.« Så trådte han hen til dobloonen på stormasten og sagde: »Mænd, dette guld er mit, for jeg har fortjent det. Men jeg lader det blive hængende her, til den hvide hval er død. Og den af jer, der først får øje på ham den dag, han bliver dræbt, ham tilhører guldet. Og hvis jeg selv får øje på ham igen den dag, skal ti gange så meget deles mellem jer alle! Af sted nu! — Dækket er dit, sir!«
Med de ord stillede han sig halvt ned i lugen, trak hatten dybt ned i panden og blev stående der til daggry, bortset fra at han nu og da rejste sig for at se, hvordan natten gik.
